newsitem.title: UK: Europe grains market sentiment improves.
newsitem.headline: Europe grains market sentiment improves.

text.p: Sentiment in Europe's grains market looked a little less sickly by the end of this week.
Traders ideas of export prospects improved, despite a lacklustre EU tender, and the lack of sellers reasserted itself as a bullish factor.
French wheat prices rose, mostly helped by fresh export prospects, dealers said.
After a dull start on Monday, Rouen wheat for February gained five francs on Thursday as traders put in large export bids at the weekly EU grain auction.
February wheat added a further 2.50 francs at 857.50 francs per tonne after traders said Iran had bought between 200,000 and 400,000 tonnes of French wheat.
"It is an unusually high tonnage for that country," one dealer said. There was no official confirmation.
Dealers largely ignored the outcome of Thursday's EU grain auction, saying the wheat rebate was in line with world prices and a firmer dollar.
Fob Atlantic prices for maize shed 10 francs on the week after the European Union cleared larger than expected preferential imports of non-EU maize into Spain.
In addition a week-long truckers strike in Spain was hampering French grain flows to Spain.
But a lack of sellers was limiting the market's downwards potential, dealers said.
On Thursday the European Union cleared the preferential import of 569,000 tonnes of non-EU maize to Spain out of an initial quota of 850,000 tonnes.
German traders report their domestic and export markets still slow amid downward pressure on prices.
Some consumers have cancelled import contracts because domestic supplies have meanwhile been offered more cheaply.
Increasing volumes of maize, barley and rye seen headed for intervention.
But sentiment is not too bearish. EU third country exports are ahead of last year and grains prices are still generally above intervention.
Poland's reinstatement of import tax is not seen affecting German or British exports too much although Denmark reportedly might have lost some sales.
Sellers expect Polish buying will be purely demand-driven and the policy may be revised at any time.
German traders reckoned that Britain seemed to have given up on some continental markets because of the pound strength.

The UK grains market remains a creature of currency moves, with many traders obliged to pay more attention to sterling/mark and sterling/franc cross rates than to the fundamental market position. "At the moment it's just bobbing along the bottom," one east of England trader said.

"If currency goes down, we'll go up," he said, stressing a firm underlying position. There was a good level of export enquiries and demand, while farmers were not bringing large amounts to the market. "The farmer is in no hurry to sell," he said.
Others agreed that the export picture is not so dismal as some think. But the rise in sterling is creating problems, especially as the market lags slightly behind sterling's rises.

"The sterling fob price is just a function of the European spot price, converted by spot sterling," one trader said. "but it's usually less competitive, because it's always catching up with the strength of sterling," he said. He described the effect as "a bit of a deterrent for exports."
Even so he agreed that demand at ports remained good.
Spanish traders said a nine-day-old truckers strike was slowing business, and prices were meaningless as no actual trades were really taking place.
But a cereal trader in the north said the strike would not start to have a big effect on prices unless it lasted until next week.
Italian cereal markets were once again calm this week with no substantial changes.

Maize prices did show a drop to a lower range. "Maize prices are still at higher levels even though the market's capacity to absorb the crop is much lower than the actual supply," the Italian Institute for Agriculture Studies (ISMEA) said.
